title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, confirmatory audit to evaluate conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy on a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample. The preregistered design (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) used a single hosted LLM (declared model: gpt-5-mini), a deterministic task generator, and a deterministic NetOps validator. Execution produced no preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator success in baseline and guarded conditions (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Crucially, the executed sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic tasks and used shared_initial_candidate generation semantics (baseline and guarded reused a single generation per item), which mechanically removed the possibility of generation‑level discordance for this run. We reconcile preregistration→execution artifacts, explain why the run was degenerate for contamination detection, and give artifact‑grounded recommendations (independent re‑generation, provenance‑rich sampling, per‑item overlap summaries, multi‑model scope, paraphrase‑robust detectors) to increase audit sensitivity in future studies.

sections.introduction:
Motivation and problem statement. Large language models (LLMs) are being adopted for NetOps tasks (intent→configuration translation, configuration repair). Valid benchmarked performance is essential to assess operational trustworthiness. Two recurring measurement risks undermine reliability claims: dataset contamination (benchmark items present in model training corpora) and construct invalidity (benchmarks composed of templated, low‑complexity tasks). Both can inflate apparent model accuracy and mislead deployment decisions.

Research question. We preregistered and executed an audit asking: under conservative deterministic contamination detectors and a guarded exclusion rule, how many high‑confidence flags arise in a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample, and how much does applying the guarded exclusion change validator‑measured success rates (primary estimand: paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline)? The preregistration specified detectors, thresholds, sampling, replacement policies, and a confirmatory paired analysis (paired_binary_analysis_v1).

Contributions and scope. We report: (1) a fully preregistered, archived confirmatory execution (study_id contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1); (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics on Npairs = 150 with deterministic validator traces; and (3) a preregistration→execution reconciliation that identifies why the run produced a degenerate null and provides artifact‑grounded design prescriptions to improve audit sensitivity. Important scope note (explicit): the executed confirmatory sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated deterministically and the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), so baseline and guarded conditions reused a single model generation per item. Those two execution facts materially limit inference: the observed zero flags and zero paired difference apply to this synthetic, shared‑generation regime and do not imply absence of contamination in independent web‑sourced benchmarks.
sections.related_work:
Positioning within NetOps and LLM evaluation literature. Prior system and benchmark work shows that LLMs can produce operationally useful network configurations in constrained settings and that integrating verifiers or iterative validate–repair loops improves average repair quality [https://openalex.org/W7157506260, https://openalex.org/W7163636922]. Deterministic network verification tools (e.g., Header Space Analysis and incremental verification methods) are practical oracles for reachability and policy checks and are commonly adopted in generate→validate workflows [http://citeseerx.ist.psu.edu/viewdoc/summary?doi=10.1.1.300.8659, https://openalex.org/W2742515467].

Meta‑evaluation literature highlights contamination and construct‑validity risks in LLM benchmarks and recommends contamination‑aware audits, per‑item overlap reporting, and conservative exclusion/retemplating procedures to avoid overclaiming model capability [https://openalex.org/W4404534210, https://openalex.org/W7166900660]. Our work complements these directions by executing a preregistered contamination audit with deterministic validators and by publishing the end‑to‑end artifacts necessary for reconciliatory analysis; unlike large capability benchmarks, our emphasis is methodological audit design and an artifact‑grounded reconciliation of preregistration and execution outcomes.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration summary and primary estimand. The study was preregistered (study_id contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1). The primary estimand is the paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) across item×model pairs; the confirmatory statistical test is exact McNemar (two‑sided) and a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI with 10,000 resamples (bootstrap_seed preregistered). The preregistration froze detector thresholds, replacement rules, sampling plan, and analysis scripts before execution.

Detectors and guarded policy (frozen). The preregistered detectors were: (1) exact normalized token equality after canonicalization; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with a preregistered high‑confidence flag threshold ≥ 0.80 and sensitivity checks at 0.65 and 0.50; and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps to model cutoff dates. The guarded policy deterministically excludes only high‑confidence flags (exact match OR 5‑gram overlap ≥ 0.80) and replaces them with deterministic retemplated/topology‑augmented items sampled from the same generator distribution under fixed seeds; replacements required an embedding similarity check before acceptance. All detector and replacement rules were archived in the transformation manifest per the preregistration.

Sampling, task generation semantics, and critical execution choices. The preregistration allowed deterministic task generators for reproducible confirmatory runs but required clear documentation when synthetic sampling or shared generation was used. The execution used deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5 to produce provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (source identifiers prefixed "synthetic‑netops:"). Crucially, execution semantics set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate): when no high‑confidence exclusions occur, a single model generation per item is reused for both baseline and guarded episodes. This setting was preregistered and is recorded in the execution manifest and model configuration.

Verification oracle and scoring rule. The validator is deterministic_netops_validator_v5. For intent→configuration tasks the validator performs parse→state‑update→property checks (reachability, workflow constraints, field‑level guards) and returns a binary pass/fail plus detailed traces (parsed command counts, touched fields, final_state). The prespecified scoring rule was full_intent_constraint_validation: a generated configuration must produce the intended final state and respect workflow policies to pass.

Analysis plan and prespecified sensitivities. The primary confirmatory analysis used paired_binary_analysis_v1. Prespecified sensitivities included: (a) treating failed model calls as failures; (b) fuzzy threshold sensitivity at 0.50/0.65/0.80; and (c) stratified analysis by templated vs realistic items. Power guidance in the preregistration described multi‑model designs capable of detecting ≈5 percentage‑point paired differences at 80% power; the single‑model single‑generation execution used here reduces sensitivity and increases the minimal detectable effect.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. The archived execution manifest records planned_episode_count = 300 (150 item pairs), completed_episode_count = 300, failed_episode_count = 0. Because independent_condition_generation = false and no high‑confidence exclusions occurred, the run used a shared generation per item and model_calls_used = 150 (one generation per item) rather than two independent generations per pair; deterministic reconciliation artifacts confirm complete_pair_count = 150 and consistent provider‑call accounting. All model calls, validator traces, and sampling seeds were archived per the preregistration.

Contamination detector outcomes and overlap reporting. The preregistered high‑confidence contamination detectors produced zero high‑confidence flags for the executed sample; the contamination_summary artifact contains no flagged episodes. Important artifact‑grounded detail: the preregistered detector implementation recorded explicit fuzzy‑overlap outputs and replacement logs only for episodes that met flagging criteria or required replacement handling. Because no episodes reached the high‑confidence threshold in this execution, the detector produced no per‑item overlap summaries or aggregated overlap distributions to include in the archive for this run. Therefore we report, per the archived records, the absence of high‑confidence flags and the archival absence of per‑item overlap distributions rather than synthesizing overlap statistics that the execution did not record.

Validator outcomes and confirmatory statistics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and for all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The paired success‑rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, preregistered seed) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode validator traces (parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state snapshots) are archived and available in the execution bundle.

Representative exemplar. A representative archived episode (pair‑000001) shows identical reference_answer and normalized_response and a validator_trace with parsed_command_count = 4 and score_reason_code = VALID_CONFIGURATION; this exemplar illustrates the artifact structure (task manifest entry, shared/condition responses, validator output) and is included in the archived artifacts.

What the results concretely show. For the executed synthetic, shared‑generation regime, the preregistered conservative detectors produced no high‑confidence contamination flags and guarded exclusions produced no change in validator pass rate. The execution artifacts mechanistically explain this outcome: provenance‑stable synthetic sampling removes likely exact/fuzzy overlap with public corpus fingerprints, and shared generation semantics produced identical outputs across conditions when no exclusion was triggered. Thus the confirmatory paired test was degenerate for detecting generation‑level contamination under these execution semantics.
sections.discussion:
Why the run was degenerate and how the artifacts support that explanation. Two execution facts—both preregistered and archived—explain the degenerate null: (1) the sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (deterministically generated), which by construction avoided high fuzzy‑overlap or exact matches to public corpus fingerprints; and (2) the run used shared_initial_candidate semantics (independent_condition_generation = false), so baseline and guarded reused the same model generation per item when no high‑confidence flags occurred. Both facts are recorded in the archived task manifest and model configuration and together made the paired comparison insensitive to generation‑level contamination signals in this execution.

Design lessons and artifact‑grounded recommendations. The preregistration→execution reconciliation yields concrete, artifact‑grounded audit improvements:
- Use provenance‑rich public benchmark items (web‑sourced) when the goal is to detect training‑data leakage; synthetic provenance undermines detector sensitivity.
- Set independent_condition_generation = true so baseline and guarded conditions use independent generations and cannot collapse via shared outputs.
- Expand to multi‑model and multi‑seed sampling to increase observable discordance and to detect model‑specific memorization patterns.
- Record per‑item fuzzy overlap scores regardless of thresholded flags to enable overlap‑distribution reporting and post‑hoc sensitivity analyses.
- Add paraphrase‑robust contamination detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases (fuzzy overlaps in [0.50, 0.80)). Each recommendation follows directly from the archived execution manifest, contamination_summary artifact, and the absence of overlap logs in this run.

Operational implications. For NetOps practitioners and benchmark curators, the audit demonstrates that contamination audits must deliberately exercise detector failure modes: sampling provenance and independent generation semantics are first‑order controls that determine whether detectors can observe leakage. Deterministic validators remain useful oracles for functional correctness but do not substitute for audit designs that can elicit contamination signals.

Threats to validity and generality. Internal validity: shared generation semantics and single‑model design reduced the experiment's ability to detect generation‑level contamination (documented by the execution manifest). Construct validity: the detector suite (exact + fuzzy 5‑gram + timestamp heuristics) is conservative and can miss paraphrased memorization; the run recorded no overlap scores for non‑flagged items, preventing distributional overlap analysis. External validity: single‑model (gpt‑5‑mini) and synthetic sampling limit generalization to other models and to public benchmarks. Conclusion validity: with all pairs concordant (n11 only), the paired test yields no discordant evidence—this is a valid but uninformative statistical outcome for the stated estimand under these execution semantics.

Recommendations for future confirmatory audits. A future confirmatory design that aims to detect contamination effects should: draw a provenance‑rich sample of web‑sourced items (with timestamped provenance), preregister independent_condition_generation = true, include multiple models or randomized seeds, persist per‑item overlap scores irrespective of flags, and plan sample sizes/power for the higher variance induced by independent regeneration and multiple models.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors in an LLM‑for‑NetOps setting. For the executed provenance‑stable synthetic sample with shared generation semantics, the detectors produced zero high‑confidence flags and the deterministic validator passed all baseline and guarded episodes (150/150 each). The artifact record makes clear that this degenerate null outcome resulted from preregistered and archived execution choices (synthetic provenance and shared generation) that reduced audit sensitivity rather than indicating an absence of contamination in independent public benchmarks. We provide artifact‑grounded recommendations—independent generation, provenance‑rich sampling, per‑item overlap logging, multi‑model scope, and paraphrase‑robust detectors—to increase audit informativeness. All experiment artifacts, validator traces, analysis inputs/outputs, and execution manifests are archived in the execution bundle and are available for verification via the recorded artifact manifest paths referenced below in the Disclosure Statement.

limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt-5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or training corpora.

Sampled items in this execution were provenance‑stable synthetic/deterministically generated tasks; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in real‑world, web‑crawled benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false), producing identical model outputs when no exclusions occurred and thus limiting sensitivity to interventions that rely on independent re‑generation.

Contamination detection used preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization, partial leakage) may escape these heuristics and require paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication.

The archive does not contain per‑item fuzzy overlap score summaries for non‑flagged episodes in this execution because the detector implementation recorded detailed overlap outputs only for flagged or replaced episodes; consequently, overlap distribution statistics could not be reported from the archived run.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of the checked functional constraints but does not imply production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's scope.
